regionalPopulation: Estimated 114 individuals (2018 Bangladesh Tiger Action Plan survey)
notes: The Sundarbans population is the only tiger population in Bangladesh. It represents a unique mangrove-adapted tiger population. Global status is EN (IUCN 2022), but Bangladesh regional assessment is CR due to extremely small population size and restricted range. In Bangladesh tigers are concentrated in the Sundarbans mangrove forest (about 60% of the roughly 10,000 km² Sundarbans lies in Bangladesh), with occasional records from the mixed-evergreen forests of the Chittagong Hill Tracts; the Sundarbans remains the priority tiger conservation landscape (IUCN Red List supplementary information, Goodrich et al.). A 2023 Forest Department–IUCN prey census led by Jahangirnagar University counted 141,357 spotted deer and 45,110 wild boar (both increased) but only 687 barking deer (crashed from 2,265 in the 1980s); spotted deer and wild boar supply about 89% of prey biomass (Aziz et al. 2020). Tigers are solitary; gestation lasts about 103–106 days with 2–3 cubs on average, and successful reproduction depends on adequate large-ungulate prey (Sunquist & Sunquist; IUCN). Conservation rests on the Wildlife Order 1973, the Bangladesh Tiger Action Plan 2018–2027, and the 2011 India–Bangladesh bilateral protocol on joint Sundarbans tiger research.

regionalPopulation: Estimated 200-350 individuals in Bangladesh (IUCN Bangladesh 2015)
notes: Small, fragmented populations in Chittagong Hill Tracts and occasional transboundary movement from India into Sylhet region. Historically more widespread. Global status is EN (IUCN 2020), but Bangladesh regional assessment is CR due to small population size and severe fragmentation. IUCN Bangladesh lists the species as Critically Endangered nationally (2000; Red List of Bangladesh 2015) against a global Endangered listing (IUCN 2020). A 2016 IUCN survey found 268 resident elephants, all in the southeast (Chittagong, Chittagong Hill Tracts, Cox’s Bazar); migratory herds also move along the northern border districts, and captive elephants are held separately. Twelve corridors were identified in 2016, one already lost to Rohingya camp construction in Cox’s Bazar. Adults consume over 150 kg of vegetation and about 140 litres of water daily, driving crop raiding (banana, rice, cassava) and retaliation; electrocution is an additionally recorded killer, with 34 elephants killed in 2021 alone. Asian elephants live in matriarchal herds from which males depart around age 10–14; gestation lasts 18–22 months (longest of any land mammal), producing a single calf of about 100 kg, and wild lifespan is about 60 years (Britannica; WCS Thailand). The species is an umbrella species for forest biodiversity, listed in CITES Appendix I and the Wildlife (Conservation) Act schedules, with actions guided by the Bangladesh Elephant Conservation Action Plan.

regionalPopulation: Widespread and relatively common; no precise population estimate
notes: Red fox occurs across much of Bangladesh in suitable habitat. More common in northern and central regions (Barind tract, haor areas). Adapts well to agricultural and peri-urban landscapes. Global status is LC (IUCN 2016), consistent with Bangladesh regional assessment. The red fox (Vulpes vulpes, Linnaeus 1758) is the world’s most widely distributed carnivore and is globally Least Concern with a stable population (IUCN 2016, amended assessment 2021); the Bangladesh national assessment is likewise Least Concern (IUCN Bangladesh 2015). It is an opportunistic omnivore — rodents (especially voles), rabbits, birds and eggs, insects, fruit and carrion — shifting seasonally, and an efficient scavenger around farms and settlements (Britannica; US Forest Service FEIS). Mating occurs in winter (January–March); after about 51–53 days of gestation the vixen bears an average of 4–5 pups in a den, often a borrowed burrow, with both parents provisioning, and young disperse in autumn (Britannica; NJDEP Fish & Wildlife). No dedicated national fox conservation programme was identified in the sources consulted; persistence in Bangladesh depends on the habitat mosaic, poultry protection, and reduced roadkill and poisoning. Bangladesh-specific diet composition is unstudied and left for formal review.

regionalPopulation: Estimated 200-400 individuals in Bangladesh (Sundarbans and haor basins)
notes: Bangladesh is a global stronghold for Fishing Cat. Sundarbans and northeast haor basins (Tanguar Haor, Hakaluki Haor) support significant populations. Listed as Vulnerable globally (IUCN 2025, assessed May 2024; previously Endangered 2008–2010) and regionally. Protected under Bangladesh Wildlife Conservation Act 2012. The Bangladesh national listing should be treated with care: project data records VU regionally while at least one secondary account reports Endangered (2015); this conflict is flagged here for formal review rather than silently resolved. Bangladesh is a global stronghold — Sundarbans plus northeast haors (Tanguar, Hakaluki, Arial Beel, Baikka Beel). A Dhaka University survey documented 361 conflicts in 2016–2021 (roughly one every two weeks) with 160 cat deaths, driven by fear and mistaken identity with tigers, revenge for poultry losses, and social pressure; infrastructure such as the Dhaka–Mawa expressway through Arial Beel fragments habitat, and pet-trade captures are evidenced (Mongabay 2024; Sultana et al. 2022). A wetland specialist and strong swimmer with partially webbed front toes, it is chiefly piscivorous (fish, shellfish, frogs) but takes birds — including colonial nesters raided from 8-metre treetops in Bangladesh — rodents, poultry and carrion (Denver Zoo; Sadik & Akash 2024). Mating occurs around January–February; gestation lasts about 63–70 days with 1–4 (usually 2) kittens, weaned at 4–6 months and independent near 10 months (Denver Zoo). The IUCN Red List records the Bengali name Baghrol (বাঘরোল), added to local names here. Conservation presence includes Project Fishing Cat Bangladesh (est. 2012, Baikka Beel, Hail Haor).
